summary: The note traces the history of Aberdeen from its early settlement to its medieval development. The city began as two separate burghs, Old Aberdeen and New Aberdeen, and received charters from William the Lion and Robert the Bruce that granted corporate rights and financial independence. It was damaged during the Wars of Scottish Independence, including the destruction of Aberdeen Castle in 1308 and a burning by Edward III in 1336, and was later fortified against neighbouring lords.
one_line: A history of Aberdeen, from its early settlement and two original burghs through medieval charters, wars of independence, and fortifications.
key_facts: The Aberdeen area has seen human settlement for at least 8,000 years.
The city began as two separate burghs: Old Aberdeen at the mouth of the river Don, and New Aberdeen, a fishing and trading settlement.
New Aberdeen was located where the Denburn waterway entered the river Dee estuary.
The earliest charter for Aberdeen was granted by William the Lion in 1179 and confirmed the corporate rights granted by David I.
In 1319, the Great Charter of Robert the Bruce transformed Aberdeen into a property-owning and financially independent community.
The Great Charter of 1319 granted the nearby Forest of Stocket, whose income formed the basis for the city's Common Good Fund.
The Common Good Fund still benefits Aberdonians, according to the note.
During the Wars of Scottish Independence, Aberdeen was under English rule.
Robert the Bruce laid siege to Aberdeen Castle before destroying it in 1308.
Robert the Bruce's forces massacred the English garrison after destroying Aberdeen Castle in 1308.
Edward III of England burned the city of Aberdeen in 1336, but it was rebuilt and extended.
Aberdeen was strongly fortified to prevent attacks by neighbouring lords.
The gates of Aberdeen were removed by 1770.
